v: Next year, Calgary wants fifteen percent more in property tax. So we asked one simple question. Is that about growth, or about spending?

Calgary has grown fast. About one point six million people now, about twenty-one percent more than in twenty twenty-one, on the City's own estimates. If growth is the reason, the numbers should line up.
So we added it up. Population growth plus inflation comes to about sixteen percent by twenty thirty. The tax plan adds about forty-four. Almost three times as much.

So what is driving the spending increase? The biggest single increase is not police, and it is not transit. It is Water Services, at forty-three percent of the increase in operating spending. But here is an important distinction. Water is mainly paid through your water bill, not property tax.
But here is the part nobody talks about. That fifteen percent is not the same for everyone.

Picture two neighbours. One owns a semi-detached house. The other owns a condo down the street. Condo values have been falling, while houses have barely moved. So the house could pay about eighteen percent more, and the condo about eight. Same city. Same budget. Very different bills.
And the growth itself? Half of it was concentrated in just five wards. Those wards have about a third fewer transit stops per person, and far fewer City recreation sites.

So, growth or spending? Growth explains part of the increase. But the proposed tax rise is much higher than the growth and inflation benchmark. That does not automatically mean the difference is waste. It means Calgarians deserve to understand what they are paying for.
And Council can still change the number. A ten percent increase instead of fifteen would mean an estimated one hundred twenty-eight million dollars less in revenue than the proposed increase.
Council debates the budget from November twenty-third. The full study, with every number, is at calgary insight dot c a. So tell us. Is fifteen percent fair? Drop your answer in the comments.
